subject: maths
stem:
Ira writes four claims about the number list 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, …

Which claim treats the list as a mathematical pattern?

options.A: The list looks neat, so it is a pattern even with no rule stated.
options.B: Explaining the list is what creates the even numbers in the first place.
options.C: Each term is 2 more than the one before, because we keep adding 2.
options.D: The same list also proves a new theorem about all infinite sequences.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar makes a tiny pencil mark on his notebook page and labels it P.

In geometry, what does this mark stand for?

options.A: A point: a precise location with no length, breadth, or thickness, named by the letter P.
options.B: A short line segment that starts at P and has a measurable length.
options.C: The black disk of graphite itself, which has a real size on the page.
options.D: Any decorative blot on the page, even when it does not name a location.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit draws a straight path that starts at point A, ends at point B, and does not continue past either point.

What has he drawn?

options.A: A line, because it is straight.
options.B: A ray starting at A and passing through B without ending.
options.C: A line segment AB, because it has two endpoints A and B.
options.D: A line segment even if he erases endpoint B and lets the path run on.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir stands in a height line with other children. The rule is: each child says the count of taller children standing immediately next to that child. Qadir says "1".

What does Qadir's "1" report?

options.A: The count of taller children standing immediately next to him.
options.B: His own height in centimetres.
options.C: The total number of children in the whole line.
options.D: How many children in the line are shorter than him.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul writes this number grid (neighbours are left, right, top, and bottom only):

4  7  3
6  9  5
2  8  1

A supercell is greater than every immediate neighbour.

Which cell is a supercell?

options.A: The cell with 9
options.B: The cell with 8
options.C: The cell with 7
options.D: The cell with 6

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma wants to answer this question: which fruit do the students in Class 6A like most for the mid-day snack?

Which plan correctly sets up the inquiry?

options.A: Treat the words Class 6A as the answer, and collect no fruit choices.
options.B: Collect fresh fruit choices from some students, without naming Class 6A.
options.C: Collect fresh fruit choices from the students in Class 6A.
options.D: First choose a fruit Uma likes, then say that Class 6A likes that fruit.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil records favourite fruits from his row: mango, apple, mango, banana, apple, mango.

How should he find which fruit is most common?

options.A: Assign each answer to one fruit category and count the frequency in each category.
options.B: Leave the answers in the order he heard them and treat that list as the finished result.
options.C: Square the number of answers and report that square as the frequency of mango.
options.D: Multiply each fruit name by how often it appears to get a total amount, skipping the frequency table.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin needs a number that is a multiple of both 4 and 6.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 8 is such a number, because 8 is a multiple of 4.
options.B: 2 is such a number, because 2 divides both 4 and 6.
options.C: 12 is such a number, because 12 is a multiple of 4 and of 6.
options.D: Any multiple of 4 alone is enough, even if it is not a multiple of 6.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia lists multiples of 4 as 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, ... and multiples of 6 as 6, 12, 18, 24, ...

What is the smallest common multiple of 4 and 6?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona's rectangular garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. She wants the distance around the garden once, along the boundary.

What is that distance?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu shares the same chapati equally. She compares the unit fractions 1/6 and 1/8 from that whole.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 1/8 is greater than 1/6 because 8 is greater than 6.
options.B: 1/6 is greater than 1/8 because fewer equal shares make each share larger.
options.C: 1/6 and 1/8 are equal because each numerator is 1.
options.D: 1/8 is greater because the denominator is the size of the share.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona and Nitin each start with the same whole chapati. Mona cuts hers into 4 equal pieces. Nitin cuts his into 4 pieces of different sizes. Each takes one piece and calls it one-fourth of the chapati.

Whose piece is a valid fractional unit of one-fourth?

options.A: Only Mona's piece, because the parts must be equal in size.
options.B: Both pieces, because each chapati was cut into 4 pieces.
options.C: Only Nitin's piece, because unequal shapes still make fourths.
options.D: Neither piece, because fourths must be triangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek opens a compass to a fixed length, keeps the metal point fixed at P, and moves only the pencil.

What path does the pencil draw?

options.A: A circle whose radius is the point P.
options.B: A circle with centre at the moving pencil tip, and with P on the rim.
options.C: A circle with centre P, and with every pencil point at the same fixed distance from P.
options.D: A square that has one corner fixed at P.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya wants a circular hole of radius 2 cm at the centre of a square card of side 10 cm. She will use a compass.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Place the compass tip at a corner of the square and set the radius to 2 cm.
options.B: Place the tip anywhere on the card; only setting the radius to 2 cm matters.
options.C: Place the tip at the centre of the square and set the radius to 2 cm.
options.D: Draw the curve freehand without a fixed centre, because neat artwork is enough.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya has a paper square with a design on it. She wants to know whether the design has mathematical symmetry.

Which check decides that?

options.A: The design looks attractive, so it is symmetric.
options.B: The design has matching colours, so it is symmetric.
options.C: A fold or a turn maps the design onto itself.
options.D: A definite pattern of matching parts is what creates symmetry by itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier has a paper heart and a possible vertical mid-line drawn on it.

When is that mid-line a line of symmetry?

options.A: Whenever the heart looks roughly balanced, even if it is never folded.
options.B: When folding along the mid-line is treated as a result produced by an already known line of symmetry.
options.C: Only when folding along that mid-line makes the two parts overlap exactly point for point.
options.D: Only when a group-theory symmetry order of 2 is named for the heart.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin marks three temperatures on a number line with 0 as the reference: −3 °C, 0 °C, and 4 °C.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: −3 °C is below zero, 4 °C is above zero, and 0 °C is neither positive nor negative.
options.B: 0 °C is a positive temperature because it is written without a minus sign.
options.C: −3 °C is above zero, and 4 °C is below zero.
options.D: −3 °C and 4 °C are the same kind of signed value because both sit away from zero.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil writes the successor of 99,999 and names the place-value unit.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The successor is 99,998.
options.B: The successor is 1,00,000, which is one crore.
options.C: The successor is 1,00,000, which is one lakh (1 followed by 5 zeroes).
options.D: 99,999 already counts as one lakh because it looks nearly as large.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia buys 3 notebooks at Rs 20 each and pays with a Rs 100 note. She writes $100 - 3 \times 20$ for the change she should receive.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 40 is the expression; $100 - 3 \times 20$ is only a name for that value.
options.B: $100 - 3 \times 20$ is an expression, but it has no value until an equals sign is written beside it.
options.C: $100 - 3 \times 20$ is an arithmetic expression for the change, and its value is 40.
options.D: The expression must be the printed 100 alone, because 100 is the largest number she sees.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit measures a pencil on a ruler marked in centimetres. The tip ends between the 7 cm and 8 cm marks.

What should he do to report the length more accurately?

options.A: Report 7 cm, because the tip has not reached 8 cm.
options.B: Split the gap into unequal marks of any sizes he likes.
options.C: Split the 1 cm gap into equal smaller parts and count how many the tip passes.
options.D: Ignore the ruler marks and use only the printed number 7 on the pencil.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul has m marbles. She buys 5 more and then gives 3 to a friend.

Which expression shows how many marbles she has now?

options.B: marbles + 5 − 3

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya draws two straight lines on her notebook page. The lines meet at exactly one point.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The lines are intersecting, and their meeting point forms four angles.
options.B: Two straight lines can meet at two different points if she extends them far enough.
options.C: Meeting at one point means the lines are parallel.
options.D: Two straight lines that meet need not form any angles at the meeting point.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier lines up four children left to right with heights 140 cm, 150 cm, 145 cm, and 155 cm. Each child calls out how many taller children stand in front of that child.

Which height-code is correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira draws a closed shape with three corner points P, Q and R joined by three straight sides.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The shape is named only by one corner point, such as P.
options.B: The shape is a triangle even if one side is left open.
options.C: The shape is triangle PQR, with three sides and three angles at P, Q and R.
options.D: The shape is a triangle because the letter R is printed largest on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar walks at a steady speed of 3/4 km each hour. He walks for 2 hours at that same rate.

What total distance does he walk?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir has two paper triangles of the same shape and size. One fits exactly over the other after he flips it.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: They are congruent only if he does not flip or rotate either triangle.
options.B: They are congruent: exact copies under superimposition, and flipping is allowed.
options.C: Same shape alone is enough for congruence even when the sizes differ.
options.D: Congruence here requires a right angle, hypotenuse, and one matching side before he can decide.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma needs an ordered pair of numbers whose sum is 10 and whose difference (first minus second) is 4.

Which ordered pair is correct?

options.B: The second number 3 alone, without a first number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin has two ribbons of lengths 18 cm and 24 cm. He wants to cut both into pieces of the same whole-number length, using the largest possible piece length with no ribbon left over.

What should he find?

options.A: A common multiple of 18 and 24.
options.B: Any common factor of 18 and 24, even if a larger one also fits.
options.C: The highest common factor of 18 and 24.
options.D: The sum of 18 and 24.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
In the decimal 36.82, each digit has a place value.

What does the digit 8 stand for?

options.A: 8 tenths
options.B: 8 hundredths
options.C: 8 ones
options.D: 8 tens

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu's teacher asks the class: "How many books do students in our class usually carry?"

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The prompt is statistical: it is about data with expected variation across students.
options.B: It is not statistical because the exact answer is not known yet.
options.C: It is only a fixed fact about one named student, so it is not statistical.
options.D: Any question that contains the word "how many" is automatically statistical.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek marks endpoints X and Y. He finds two points P and Q so that each is the same distance from X as from Y. He draws the line through P and Q.

What is that line?

options.A: The line that must pass through the endpoints X and Y only.
options.B: A line that creates equal distances from X and Y after it is drawn.
options.C: The perpendicular bisector of segment XY.
options.D: A guide for tiling a rectangle with 2 by 1 tiles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya has a weighing scale that is balanced. The left pan holds one sealed packet and a 20 g weight. The right pan holds a 50 g weight.

How can she find the mass of the packet?

options.A: Remove the 20 g weight from the left pan only, then read the right pan.
options.B: Add the packet mass to both pans so the scale tips.
options.C: Remove 20 g from each pan so the packet alone balances a 30 g weight.
options.D: Compare the pans while the scale is tipped and unbalanced.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
A school has lockers numbered 1 to 9, all starting closed. Student 1 toggles every locker. Student 2 toggles every 2nd locker. Student 3 toggles every 3rd, and so on, up to student 9.

After every student has finished, which lockers are open?

options.A: Lockers 1, 4, and 9
options.B: Lockers 2, 3, 5, and 7
options.D: Lockers 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil folds a sheet so each fold doubles the current thickness. The starting thickness is 0.1 mm. He wants the thickness after k folds.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Add 2 mm at each fold to the starting thickness.
options.B: Multiply the starting thickness by k only, ignoring that each fold acts on the current thickness.
options.C: Replace "double" with "add two" and sum 0.1 + 2 + 2 + … for k folds.
options.D: Start at 0.1 mm and multiply by 2 at each fold (repeated multiplication).

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia counts seven pebbles by matching each pebble to one clap in order, from clap 1 through clap 7.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The ordered clap sequence alone counts the pebbles even if some pebbles are skipped.
options.B: One-to-one matching works only with written Hindu numerals, not with claps.
options.C: Each pebble is matched exactly once to one clap, so the ordered claps show that there are seven pebbles.
options.D: Seven is correct because the word seven is the largest word written on the board.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul sorts four closed shapes: a square; a triangle; a circle; and a five-sided polygon with straight sides.

Which shape is a quadrilateral?

options.A: The square
options.B: The triangle
options.C: The circle
options.D: The five-sided polygon

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya keeps the four numbers 3, 4, 5 and 6 fixed. She only changes the + and − signs between them, writing expressions of the form 3 ± 4 ± 5 ± 6.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Every such value has the same parity; for these four consecutive numbers that common parity is even.
options.B: Changing one sign can flip the parity of the value.
options.C: The common parity depends on a sign written before the first number 3.
options.D: Parity here is settled by whether 3 divides each partial sum.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier multiplies the outside factor through the bracket: $3(x - 4)$.

Which expansion is correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira mixes juice and water in the ratio 2 : 5.

What does this ratio mean?

options.A: For every 5 parts of juice there are 2 parts of water.
options.B: Juice and water are equal, because a ratio always means equal shares.
options.C: For every 2 parts of juice there are 5 parts of water.
options.D: The whole mix is divided by adding 2 and 5 only after swapping the order.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona reads the statement "40% of the class." The whole is the class.

How should 40% be read?

options.A: 40/100 of the class
options.B: 100/40 of the class
options.C: 40 of the class, with no whole chosen
options.D: 40 more students than the whole class

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir has a square of side 3 cm. He makes a new square whose side is 6 cm, so the side length is multiplied by 2.

Which statement about the area is correct?

options.A: The area becomes 2 times as large, matching the side factor.
options.B: The area stays the same because both figures are still squares.
options.C: The area becomes 4 times as large, because area scales with the square of the side factor.
options.D: The perimeter becomes 4 times as large, and that same factor rule applies to area.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma compares the two-term ratios 2:5 and 4:10.

Which decision is correct?

options.A: They are proportional because both ratios mention corresponding terms.
options.B: They are proportional even if the second ratio is read as 10:4.
options.C: They are proportional because $2 \times 10 = 5 \times 4$.
options.D: They are proportional only when every ingredient of a full mixture matches, not just these two terms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin studies a fern leaf in which each leaflet looks like a smaller copy of the whole leaf. He also looks at a plain rectangle with no smaller copies inside it.

Which claim about the fern leaf is correct?

options.A: It is a fractal, because the same pattern repeats at smaller scales.
options.B: It is a fractal, because any leaf counts as a fractal.
options.C: It is not a fractal, because only computer drawings can be fractals.
options.D: It is not a fractal, because the plain rectangle is the true fractal pattern.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu's marks on five quizzes are 8, 8, 9, 10 and 10.

Which statement about the mean is correct?

options.A: Use only the distinct marks 8, 9 and 10, so divide their sum by 3.
options.B: Mean = (8 + 8 + 9 + 10 + 10) / 5, counting each repeated mark.
options.C: The mean is the middle mark 9, without summing.
options.D: Find the mean by multiplying the five marks instead of dividing their sum by 5.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek tracks a number trick with one letter-number x for the starting number, kept the same through every step: multiply by 2, add 6, divide by 2, then subtract the starting number.

What does this tracking show?

options.A: x is only a label for letter-number, so it cannot appear in the arithmetic steps.
options.B: After adding 6 he should switch to a new letter y for the remaining steps.
options.C: The expression simplifies to 3, so every starting number gives the final result 3.
options.D: He must also use a right-triangle length rule to finish the proof.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya cuts a paper rectangle into two pieces and rearranges the pieces into a new shape with no gaps and no overlaps.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The new shape must have smaller area, because the outline looks different.
options.B: Equal area is what forces the new shape to be a rectangle again.
options.C: The new shape has the same area as the original rectangle.
options.D: Area stays equal even if she throws one piece away before rearranging.

author: grok
